name: Qigong
origin: An ancient Chinese practice, older than tai chi and one of the historical roots of traditional Chinese medicine, that spread widely in China from the early 1980s and then around the world.
summary: Qigong is a family of Chinese mind-body exercises that coordinate posture or slow movement, breathing and a calm, focused mind, which Chinese medicine calls the three regulations of body, breath and mind. Moving forms include Baduanjin (Eight Section Brocade, eight gentle movements with stretching and controlled breathing), Wuqinxi (Five Animals), Yijinjing and Guolin qigong, while static forms hold still, meditative standing or sitting postures. Tai chi is a close relative, but it is usually a long, complex choreographed sequence, whereas health qigong is simple, repetitive and quick to learn.
theoryOfChange: Traditional Chinese medicine explains qigong as cultivating and balancing qi, a vital life energy. In modern terms it combines gentle exercise with slow breathing and meditative attention, which researchers think may shift the nervous system toward rest and recovery: some trials report lower heart rate and blood pressure, and one small trial found lower adrenaline and noradrenaline than in a wait-list group. Because it blends exercise with relaxation, it may also help mood and stress through the same routes as other exercise and relaxation practices, but these are proposed explanations, not established mechanisms.
whatYouDo: Most sessions follow a set sequence of simple, repeated movements, such as the eight movements of Baduanjin, done slowly and in time with the breath while attention rests on the body. Static forms instead hold still standing or seated postures with breath awareness, and some styles add gentle shaking or slow walking. It is usually learned in a group class with a trained instructor and then practiced at home, standing or seated.
typicalDose: Usually taught by an instructor, often in groups, with home practice in some programs. In the Baduanjin trials, sessions lasted 20 to 90 minutes, 2 to 7 times a week, for 2 to 40 weeks; more total hours went with lower anxiety and more sessions with lower depression, but the reviewers found the range too wide to recommend a specific dose.

evidence.summary: Meta-analyses of small randomized trials report less depression and anxiety, including with Baduanjin: a review of 26 trials in people with physical or mental illness, all run in mainland China or Hong Kong, found large pooled effects once studies with extreme results were set aside (15 trials pooled for anxiety and 17 for depression; one large trial set aside from the anxiety pool had a smaller effect), but the authors flag high risk of bias and that Baduanjin was often combined with other treatments (Zou and colleagues, 2018). An earlier review of 15 qigong studies could pool only 3 of them, found small effects and rated the methods poor (Wang and colleagues, 2013). For blood pressure, a review of 20 trials in 2,349 people with hypertension found large drops compared with no treatment but smaller ones than regular exercise for systolic pressure (Xiong and colleagues, 2015), while a Cochrane review on preventing heart disease saw lower blood pressure in only 3 of 6 trials and had very low confidence in the results because most trials were at high risk of bias (Hartley and colleagues, 2015). An overview of systematic reviews concluded that the evidence rests mostly on poor quality research (Lee, Oh and Ernst, 2011), so benefits look likely but their size is uncertain.

goodFitFor: People who want gentle, low-impact exercise that also calms the mind, including older adults, beginners and people living with chronic illness or limited fitness. It suits those who like a simple routine to repeat alone or in a group, and people who would rather meditate while moving than sit still.
cautions: Qigong is generally safe: few trials tracked side effects, but those that did reported no serious ones, and the main risks are those of gentle exercise, so adapt movements to your body and keep up any prescribed treatment. Inappropriate practice has been linked to qigong deviation, unusual mental and bodily reactions that can include psychosis, often in people who were already vulnerable (a causal link is hard to prove), so anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice first and learn from an experienced teacher. Be cautious about claims that qigong cures disease, which the research does not support.
namingNote: Qigong (also written qi gong or chi kung) is an umbrella term for thousands of styles; this entry covers internal, health-oriented qigong that people practice themselves, with Baduanjin as a widely studied example. Tai chi is closely related, and many scholars count it as a type of qigong, but it is treated as a separate practice here, and the evidence summary uses qigong trials only. External qigong, in which a practitioner claims to send healing qi into another person, is not included.
